title: Install
text:
Written for version 0.1.5. Commands checked on 10 November 2026; see What’s been tested for exactly how. Menus change; if what you see differs, tell the maintainer through a GitHub issue.
Installing the plugin gives the assistant instructions only. It adds no access to your files, accounts or computer; what the assistant can reach is set in the app.
The repository is its own marketplace (a marketplace is a list of plugins kept in a GitHub repository), so every route below starts from VagishHemmige/figure-design.
Pick the assistant you use.

title: Install
section: Claude (on the web, the desktop app or Cowork)
text:
Claude (on the web, the desktop app or Cowork)
You need a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise).
Add the plugin’s marketplace:

In Claude, open Settings, then Customize.
Open the Plugins tab.
Click Add, then Add marketplace.
Choose Add from a repository.
Type VagishHemmige/figure-design and confirm.

If your organization limits which marketplaces you can add, Claude will refuse it; ask your administrator.
Install the plugin:

Still in Customize → Plugins, open the Discover tab.
Select Interactive Figure Design and click Add.

These are the same steps as for R Analysis Workflow, which has screenshots. Source: Anthropic, Use plugins in Claude. Not yet tried in the Claude app with this plugin.

title: Install
text:
Claude Code
You need Claude Code version 2.1.292 or later for the one-line install. In your terminal (not inside a Claude Code session):
claude plugin install figure-design --marketplace VagishHemmige/figure-design
On an older version, use two commands instead:
claude plugin marketplace add VagishHemmige/figure-design
claude plugin install figure-design@figure-design
To check, run claude plugin list: you should see figure-design@figure-design. The plugin loads the next time you start Claude Code. To update later:
claude plugin update figure-design@figure-design
Sources: Claude Code docs, Install and manage plugins and Create a marketplace.

title: Install
text:
Codex
In your terminal:
codex plugin marketplace add VagishHemmige/figure-design
codex plugin add figure-design@figure-design
To check, run codex plugin list: you should see figure-design@figure-design as installed, enabled. To pick up a new version, run codex plugin marketplace upgrade figure-design.
Source: OpenAI, Build plugins.

title: Install
text:
ChatGPT
In ChatGPT you make the plugin with OpenAI’s Plugin Creator, pointing it at this repository. Whether Plugin Creator is available depends on your plan and workspace.

Start a new conversation.
Type @, search for Plugin Creator, and select it.
Ask it, in your own words: Create a plugin from https://github.com/VagishHemmige/figure-design.
Answer its questions and follow its prompts. Check that the name is Interactive Figure Design.

Use it: in a new conversation, type @, start typing “Interactive Figure Design”, and select it under Plugins.
Not yet tried from this repository. The plugin was first built in ChatGPT, and the same route works for R Analysis Workflow.

title: Inspection checklist
text:
Written for version 0.1.6. Source: inspection-checklist.md.
The assistant runs these checks on the rendered figure before showing it to you. They add no extra approval steps; How it works sets those.

title: Inspection checklist
text:
Content and connections

Each view says what was agreed, including the decisions and exceptions it needs.
Planned, live and unconfirmed behaviour are told apart, and each output shows only the sources that really feed it.
Every arrow is traced end to end: right start, right end, right direction, right meaning. Equivalent inputs don’t look like a sequence.
Objects that appear in several views have the same label, look and role in each.
A prerequisite sits beside the step it affects, not in an unrelated footer.

title: Inspection checklist
section: Geometry, checked by code where practical
text:
Geometry, checked by code where practical

Text and images fit their boxes and the canvas, with nothing clipped or overlapping.
No collisions between text and icons, labels and arrows, or arrows and boxes, apart from intended arrow ends (rules A5, A6 and T2).
Junctions, arrowheads, crossings, reversals and avoidable bends are inspected (A3, A4, A7, A9, A10 and A11).
Columns line up; padding and spacing are consistent (L1, L2 and L4).
Every connector, layout and label rule on Design principles is applied, and each finding names the rule it breaks. After a revision, the rules are re-checked for everything that moved and its neighbours.
The SVG parses, every referenced asset exists, and exports match the current source.

A passing geometry check isn’t proof of good design, and a trivial edit doesn’t need a test harness.

title: Inspection checklist
text:
Looking at it

At its intended size, the main action is obvious, the start and end are clear, grouping helps, and contrast is enough.
No crowded boxes next to large empty areas; fix the layout before adding more arrow routing.
Illustrations match each other and mean something; logos are genuine.
Phone width is checked honestly. If it’s illegible, there’s an enlarged view or agreed crops, keeping the approved illustration.
Every changed view and export is re-inspected; old screenshots don’t count.

title: Inspection checklist
text:
Independent review for substantial work
The reviewer gets the current render, the content brief, the style reference, the target size and the planned-versus-live distinctions. They report where each problem is, what it is, why it matters and the smallest fix, without changing the content. Factual review is kept separate from visual design review. Minor edits don’t trigger a full review.

title: Inspection checklist
text:
Interactive and delivery checks
When the figure is interactive: exact-region highlight, complete hover, moving the pointer into the panel, click to pin, touch, keyboard and focus, Escape or close, zoom and pan, behaviour at the screen edges, and scrolling, in every view. The text account and static exports stay current.
The figure is shown through the chat’s own viewer; local file links are extra, not something a phone can open. The assistant reports which browsers and devices it actually tested, which tests were simulated, and what it couldn’t check.

title: Design principles
text:
Written for version 0.1.6. Source: design-principles.md.
These are practical uses of established guidance, not rigid rules about appearance. The plugin uses them to find specific communication problems, never to strip out needed content or restyle a figure you’ve accepted.

title: Design principles
text:
Composition before decoration
Choose an orientation and reading order that show the relationships. Steps in sequence line up; equivalent inputs get equal weight; exceptions sit beside the step they affect. Leave room for branching and merging arrows before placing boxes. Avoid unnecessary crossings, bends and reversals. Use clear junctions and arrowheads; two things being close together must not be the only sign that they’re related.
Background: yWorks on layered graph layout and orthogonal edge routing. These describe the ideas; the plugin doesn’t need their software, and automatic layouts still have to be inspected.

title: Design principles
text:
Connectors and arrows
Version 0.1.6 turns the principles above into numbered rules, so a check or a reviewer can cite the rule a figure breaks. The assistant applies them when drawing, and again after any revision that moves a box or a line. Rules marked code can be checked by a script on the rendered SVG; rules marked look need judgment. The distances are the plugin’s defaults and can change for a particular figure.








Rule
What it says
Check




A1
Each arrow shows one real relationship and points the way the thing moves.
look


A2
If an arrow’s meaning isn’t obvious from its ends, label it on the arrow, not in a legend.
look


A3
Remove crossings by moving boxes before rerouting lines; aim for none.
code


A4
An unavoidable crossing is at a right angle, away from labels and arrowheads, with a gap or contrasting colours, so it can’t be read as a junction.
code and look


A5
A line never passes through a box, icon or text it doesn’t connect to, and keeps 8 px from them.
code


A6
Parallel lines stay 8 px apart and never share a path unless they deliberately merge.
code


A7
Straight or right-angled lines, with at most two bends (three along an outer channel).
code


A8
Arrows meet a box at the middle of a side, on the side facing the flow.
code


A9
Arrowheads touch the target’s edge, and lines start at the source’s edge.
code


A10
Branches and merges use one trunk and a visible junction dot; a plain crossing never has a dot.
code and look


A11
The main flow runs one way; return arrows go around the outside.
look


A12
Two-way arrows only for genuinely two-way relationships.
look


A13
Each line style has one meaning, explained once in a key.
code


A14
Long routes run along open channels, or use labelled connectors such as “to 6”.
look

title: Design principles
text:
Layout, alignment and labels








Rule
What it says
Check




L1
Boxes in a row or column line up, within 2 px.
code


L2
Equal gaps between stages; bigger gaps between groups than within them.
code


L3
Boxes are sized to their text at final size; text is never shrunk to fit.
code


L4
Nothing within 12 px of the edge, and nothing clipped.
code


L5
No crowded region beside a large empty one.
look


L6
Reading order follows the flow; stages are numbered when order matters.
look


T1
Labels are horizontal.
code


T2
No line runs through text.
code


T3
Each label sits closest to what it names.
code


T4
Text meets the destination’s minimum size: 8 pt in print, about 11 px on screen.
code



These rules are the plugin’s own synthesis, not a published standard. They restate the principles on this page and the lessons from earlier figures, add common diagramming conventions, and were adjusted after checking them against the TransplantID reference, which uses contrasting colours at crossings and long routes along open channels. Bang Wong’s Points of View columns in Nature Methods, such as “Arrows” and “Layout” (both 2011), are related reading that hasn’t yet been checked against these rules.

title: Design principles
text:
Hierarchy and grouping
Make the main explanation dominate through size, position, contrast and white space. Group related elements by placing them close together or inside a shared region. Keep alignment and spacing consistent. Important distinctions shouldn’t rely on colour alone. Setup steps and footnotes shouldn’t look as important as the central action.
Background: Nielsen Norman Group on principles of visual design, proximity and visual hierarchy.

title: Design principles
text:
Text, illustrations and shared objects
Use a restrained set of type sizes, readable line lengths and clear space around labels. Measure the rendered text and make the container fit it, rather than shrinking the text until it fits. The same object has the same role, colour and illustration in every view. Illustrations other than logos form one family; logos are authentic and their source is kept. Decoration must not change what the figure says.

title: Design principles
text:
Audience and medium
Choose the content and the way it’s drawn for the reader and where they’ll see it. The overview has to work before anything is clicked. A large figure scaled down can be technically complete and still unreadable, so inspect it at the size it will be seen, and plan enlarged viewing or section crops when needed.
Background: Rougier, Droettboom and Bourne, “Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures” (PLOS Computational Biology, 2014). That paper is general advice for scientific figures, not a standard for workflow diagrams; the plugin’s checks are its own summary rather than rules quoted from any one source.

title: Make a static figure
text:
Written for version 0.1.5.
Stages 1 to 4 of How it works. The result is one approved static SVG for each view.

title: Make a static figure
text:
Ask
Say what you want explained, in your own words. For example:

“Draw a figure explaining how our weekly literature search works, for clinicians who’ll use the results.”
“I need a diagram of the study design for the methods page: two arms, a run-in period, and the follow-up visits.”

If you already have an exact outline, paste it and say “draw this”. The assistant treats an exact outline you supply as confirmed.

title: Make a static figure
Make a static figure
text:
Confirm the outline
Before drawing, the assistant writes each view as a plain-language outline: who does what, inputs, decisions, what is read or saved, outputs, and waits. It marks what is live, planned or not yet confirmed.
Read it as you would a colleague’s description of your process. This is where most later rounds are saved: a wrong step caught here is one sentence to fix, not a redrawn figure.

title: Make a static figure
text:
Approve each SVG
The assistant draws each view, checks the rendered picture, and for a substantial figure gets an independent design review when the app allows. Then it shows you each view in the chat.
Say plainly which views you approve. Approving the content earlier, or simply not replying, does not count as approving the picture. You can skip this checkpoint, but only by saying so; it’s never assumed.
For a small change later (a word, a logo, spacing), the assistant makes the change and checks it; it doesn’t restart the questions or the full review.

title: Make a static figure
text:
Tips

Say who will read it and where. A slide, a printed page and a phone each need different text sizes.
Point out what’s wrong, not just that it’s wrong. “Arrow from B goes to the wrong box” is faster than “the flow looks off”.

title: Put it on a Quarto site
text:
Written for version 0.1.5.
Part of stage 6 of How it works. Ask for it when the figure will live on a Quarto website, such as an analysis project’s explainer site.
crumbs: Put it on a Quarto site

title: Put it on a Quarto site
text:
Ask
“Give me this figure ready for my Quarto site.” Say which site and page if the assistant can see the repository.
crumbs: Put it on a Quarto site

title: Put it on a Quarto site
text:
What you get

The files: the SVG for a static figure, or the HTML, scripts and assets for an interactive one, avoiding servers or extensions it doesn’t need.
A minimal example of how to include it on a page.
A deliberate choice between embedding the figure directly in the page and loading it in an iframe. The assistant makes this choice on purpose rather than by default.

It checks the paths, that the assets are copied when the site renders, the height on the page, and that the figure still works after Quarto renders the page. It doesn’t assume an existing hotspot extension reproduces the design without checking.
crumbs: Put it on a Quarto site

title: Put it on a Quarto site
text:
A static figure
A static SVG goes on a page like any image:
![What the figure shows, in one sentence.](images/my-figure.svg){fig-alt="A full description for screen readers."}
The figure on How it works is included exactly this way.

title: Put it on a Quarto site
text:
Publishing
The assistant publishes only what you’ve authorised, and tells you the result, anything it couldn’t check, and any decision still open.

title: How it works
text:
Written for version 0.1.5.
The plugin has one skill, figure-to-interactive. It takes a figure through up to six stages, and two of them wait for you. A static-only figure ends at stage 4; stages 5 and 6 happen only if you ask for an interactive version. Select the figure to enlarge it.

title: How it works
text:
The stages

Agree on the content. For a new figure, the assistant asks at most three questions at a time: who the figure is for, which situations it must cover, and how many views it needs. It then writes a plain-language outline of each view: who does what, what is read or saved, the decisions, and the outputs. You confirm the outline. Agreeing on tab names is not agreeing on what’s in them.
Design the flow, then the SVG. The layout comes from the relationships: steps in order, equal inputs side by side, exceptions next to the step they affect, and space kept for arrows. Then it draws one static SVG for each view.
Inspect and review. The assistant checks the rendered picture for clipped or overlapping text, wrong or misleading arrows, and hierarchy. For a substantial figure it asks a separate reviewer for a design review when the app allows that, and says so if it can’t.
Approve each SVG. Each view is shown in the chat. You approve each one. Content approval or silence doesn’t count, and nothing interactive is built until every view is approved. If you only asked for a static figure, it ends here.
Add interactivity, if you ask. Hover on a desktop, tap on a phone and keyboard access reveal more detail, without changing the approved figure.
Verify and deliver. The assistant tests what applies, says which tests were on real devices or browsers and which were simulated, and hands over the files, with a Quarto example if you want one.

You can skip either checkpoint, but only by saying so. The assistant never assumes you’ve waived one, and time passing isn’t approval.

title: How it works
text:
Where the rules live
The stages above summarise the skill file, SKILL.md. It is the authoritative version; the reference pages explain the principles and checks it relies on.

title: Make it interactive
text:
Written for version 0.1.5.
Stage 5 of How it works. It starts only after you’ve approved every static view, and only if you ask for it.

title: Make it interactive
text:
Ask
“Now make the approved figure interactive.” If you want something specific, such as one view per tab, say so.

title: Make it interactive
text:
What you get
The approved figure stays the figure. Regions of it open to show more detail:

On a desktop, hovering briefly over a region opens its full explanation; you can move the pointer into it, and click to keep it open.
On a phone, tapping the whole region opens the same content.
With a keyboard, each region is a normal focusable control with a visible focus outline, and panels close with Escape where that applies.

Only the region you selected is highlighted. Panels shouldn’t flicker, cover what you tapped, or close by accident.
If the whole figure is too small to read at phone width, the assistant adds a way to enlarge or pan it, or agreed crops of each section. It doesn’t swap your illustrated figure for a text list unless you agree. There is always a plain-text account of the content for screen readers and for anyone who can’t hover.

title: Make it interactive
text:
What stays fixed
The approved composition, illustrations, colours, relationships and content don’t change. A new view goes back through content confirmation and SVG approval; small refinements to one view don’t reopen the others.

title: Make it interactive
text:
Testing
The assistant tests hover, pinning, closing, keyboard, touch, zoom, the edges of the screen, scrolling and links, as far as it can. It tells you which tests were on a real phone or browser and which were simulated.

title: The house style
text:
Written for version 0.1.5. Source: reference-assets.md and design-lessons.md.
The plugin’s default look comes from one real figure: the maintainer’s illustrated workflow for an automated curation system for TransplantID.net. Before a substantial new design, the assistant renders and studies it rather than working from a remembered description.

title: The house style
text:
What the style is

Numbered pastel phases, each a group of related steps.
Strong navy headings and short, informative bullets.
Meaningful small illustrations from one consistent family, matched to the subject: teaching pictures for teaching, documents for CVs, browsers for websites.
Recognisable logos of the services actually involved.
Clearly directed, labelled arrows, with pending and decision paths drawn so they look different.

It is deliberately information-rich. The plugin is told not to turn it into sparse cards or another look just to satisfy a general rule, and to explain the trade-off when a change would help.

title: The house style
section: What it borrows and what it doesn’t
text:
What it borrows and what it doesn’t
The assistant reuses the visual language and adapts the layout and content to the new subject. It doesn’t copy the transplant content, and it builds new, editable text and shapes rather than reusing the reference’s artwork.
The reference figure itself is not shown on this site. It contains embedded artwork, logos and a font, and the plugin’s notes say the reference gives no new right to redistribute them, so it is used only as a reference inside the plugin.

title: The house style
text:
The interactive model
After the static figure is approved, the default model for an interactive version is the reference’s companion website: the illustrated overview stays the anchor, and regions expand on hover or tap. The plugin’s notes say that site’s late hover changes were never fully tested on phones or across browsers, so the assistant checks the new version itself rather than assuming the reference works everywhere.

title: The house style
text:
Lessons from earlier figures

A figure can render perfectly and still be wrong. One needed the actual weekly list of actions and the first-use steps, not just a diagram of approvals.
Fixing awkward arrows one by one usually means the layout is wrong. Rearrange the stages first.
Mixing shaded icons with simple line drawings looks disjointed. Logos can differ; other illustrations should match each other.
A website drawn as an empty rectangle looks unfinished next to a detailed one.
Links to files on a Windows computer didn’t open on a phone; a static SVG shown in the chat did.

text:
Not installed
site/ is the source of this website, and .github/workflows/publish.yml publishes it. .github/workflows/check.yml runs .github/scripts/check_versions.py on every pull request: it fails if the three plugin.json files disagree on name or version, if a marketplace file doesn’t list the plugin or stops pointing at plugin/, if plugin/LICENSE differs from LICENSE, or if a site page claims a newer version than the plugin. None of these is part of the plugin’s instructions.

title: What’s been tested
text:
The workflow itself
The plugin comes from the maintainer’s own figures, including the TransplantID workflow; its lessons record what went wrong along the way. It has not been tested in a structured way, and no one else has used it yet.

title: What’s been tested
text:
This site
First published by the Publish website action on 10 November 2026 with Quarto 1.8.25, and checked live. Moved to Quarto 1.12.1 the same day (#21): rendered with both versions, every page’s text is the same apart from a new “Skip to main content” link and the site title, which 1.8.25 left out of the desktop sidebar; no page scrolls sideways at phone width. The workflow figure on How it works was checked at desktop and phone widths; at phone width its one-line descriptions are small, so the page repeats every stage in text.

title: Interactive Figure Design
text:
Written for version 0.1.5.
An early version. It comes from the maintainer’s own figures, such as the TransplantID workflow; it has not yet been used by other people.

title: Interactive Figure Design
text:
What it is
Interactive Figure Design is a plugin for ChatGPT and Claude. A plugin is a set of instructions the assistant reads when a task calls for them, so it works the same way every time and in every chat. This one is for explanatory figures: workflow diagrams, study designs, system overviews and similar pictures that explain how something works.
With the plugin installed, you ask in plain words (“Draw a figure explaining how our weekly literature search works”) and the assistant follows the plugin’s steps.
It’s built for explaining processes, not plotting data: a plot of real numbers is better made by the analysis code that produces it.

title: Interactive Figure Design
text:
What it does differently
Without instructions, an assistant tends to draw first and ask later, which is why explanatory figures often take many rounds. The plugin changes the order:

Content before drawing. The assistant writes out, in plain language, what each view of the figure will explain, and you confirm it before anything is drawn.
Static before interactive. Each view is first a static SVG you can look at and approve. Interactivity comes only after that, and only if you ask.
Checked before shown. The assistant inspects the rendered picture, not just its code, and gets an independent design review for substantial figures when it can.
Your style, not a generic one. The default look is the information-rich style of the maintainer’s TransplantID figure: numbered pastel phases, strong headings, meaningful small illustrations and clearly labelled arrows.

How it works shows the six stages.

title: Interactive Figure Design
text:
Where to start

Install the plugin.
Then make a static figure, and if you want, make it interactive or put it on a Quarto site.
To see what the assistant reads, start with the house style.

title: Interactive Figure Design
text:
Before you rely on it
The plugin guides an assistant; it does not check your facts. Review what the figure says as you would a colleague’s draft before it goes into a paper, a talk or a website. What’s been tested lists what has and has not been checked.
The source, including every instruction the assistant reads, is on GitHub. Original text and code are MIT licensed; the bundled reference figure is not covered (see the house style).
